source.title: Check if it is Possible to Split Array

teaching.hint: In a successful sequence of splits, consider the last length-two piece before it becomes two singletons.

solution_outline.decisive_insight: For arrays longer than two, complete splitting is possible exactly when some originally adjacent pair sums to at least m.
solution_outline.approach: Return true immediately for length one or two. Otherwise scan adjacent pairs and return true if any pair reaches m; return false if none does.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: A qualifying adjacent pair can be kept together while positive-valued elements are peeled from the ends as good singletons; the remaining piece stays good because it contains that pair.
solution_outline.correctness: Sufficiency follows by repeatedly peeling outer singletons until only the qualifying pair remains, then splitting it. Necessity follows from any successful split tree: a deepest internal node is an original adjacent pair and, when n>2, was produced as a non-root good piece, so its sum must reach m. Lengths at most two need no qualifying pair because every required result is a singleton.
solution_outline.complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space for n elements.
solution_outline.pitfall: A large total sum does not help if no adjacent pair can serve as the final good length-two piece.

common_wrong_turns: Require the original array itself to be good
source_fidelity_notes: Long split sequences were omitted; contiguity, both-piece goodness, singleton exception, positive values, and bounds were retained.
